Auxiliary Analyses for Latent Classes

Source: vignettes/lca_auxiliary.Rmd
lca_auxiliary.Rmd

Latent class analysis (LCA) and latent profile analysis (LPA) identify unobserved groups using a set of observed indicator variables. Often, researchers also have research questions about variables that were not used to define the classes. These are called auxiliary variables. A distal outcome is an auxiliary variable considered as an outcome; other auxiliary variables may be predictors or covariates.

This vignette introduces three approaches in tidySEM: BCH, two-step maximum likelihood, and pseudo-class draws. We illustrate class-specific means, category probabilities, regressions, hypothesis tests, and predictors of class membership. For an introduction to estimating the measurement model, see Introduction to Latent Class Analysis.

The Naive Approach

An often-heard question is: Why can we not simply assign every participant to their most likely class, and use class membership as a variable in auxiliary analyses?

The reason is that latent class membership is uncertain, and based on posterior class probabilities. A participant with posterior class probabilities (.05,.93,.02)(.05,.93,.02) is most likely to belong to class 2, with high certainty. However, a participant with posterior class probabilities (.45,.35,.20)(.45,.35,.20) is most likely to belong to class 1, but there is a lot of uncertainty with this assignment.

If we treat class assignments as an observed variable, this uncertainty propagates into auxiliary analyses and biases the results and their standard errors. The three approaches below address this uncertainty in different ways.

Example: Caregiver profiles

We use the zegwaard_carecompass data included in tidySEM. As explained in the vignette on Confirmatory LCA, the measurement model uses four caregiver-experience indicators. For the present analyses, auxiliary variables concern the caregiver and the person receiving care. One requirement of all analyses presented here is that the auxiliary data must have the same number of rows in exactly the same order as the measurement data.

library(tidySEM)
library(OpenMx)
#> To take full advantage of multiple cores, use:
#>   mxOption(key='Number of Threads', value=parallel::detectCores()) #now
#>   Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS=parallel::detectCores()) #before library(OpenMx)
df <- zegwaard_carecompass
indicators <- c("burdened", "trapped", "negaffect", "loneliness")
measurement_data <- df[, indicators]

For the examples in this vignette, we will just fit a simple two-class model:

set.seed(297)
lpa_model <- mx_profiles(measurement_data, classes = 2)
saveRDS(lpa_model, cache_file("measurement"))
lpa_model <- read_cached("measurement")
table_fit(lpa_model)
#>   Minus2LogLikelihood   n Parameters observedStatistics  df RMSEASquared
#> 1                4063 513         13               2030 500            0
#>   RMSEANull   modelName  AIC  BIC saBIC Classes Entropy prob_min prob_max n_min
#> 1      0.05 equal var 2 4089 4144  4103       2    0.74     0.91     0.93  0.42
#>   n_max    LL
#> 1  0.58 -2031

Classification uncertainty 

cp <- class_prob(lpa_model)
head(cp$individual)
cp$mostlikely.class
#>      class1 class2 predicted
#> [1,] "0.69" "0.31" "1.00"   
#> [2,] "0.00" "1.00" "2.00"   
#> [3,] "0.77" "0.23" "1.00"   
#> [4,] "0.05" "0.95" "2.00"   
#> [5,] "0.16" "0.84" "2.00"   
#> [6,] "1.00" "0.00" "1.00"
#>           assigned.1 assigned.2
#> avgprob.1 "0.93"     "0.07"    
#> avgprob.2 "0.09"     "0.91"

This table shows the average probability that individuals belong to each true class (rows), and their probability of being assigned to each class (columns). The diagonal of this table thus represents the probability that observations in each class will be correctly classified. These probabilities are high, but not perfect. As also indicated in the fit table by a low Entropy criterion, these classes are not perfectly separated. Therefore, do not treat assigned class as an observed variable; these classification errors would influence downstream auxiliary analyses.

BCH: class differences in distal outcomes

The Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars (BCH) procedure first estimates the measurement model, then estimates an auxiliary multi-group model, accounting for classification uncertainty by weighting case contributions to each class’ group. In tidySEM, BCH() can compare classes on a single numeric or ordered outcome, or an entire auxiliary structural equation model.

Continuous distal outcome

Here we compare caregiver distance across classes. The default numeric-outcome specification estimates class-specific means and variances.

bch_mean <- BCH(lpa_model, data = df$distance)
table_results(bch_mean, columns = NULL)
#>              label lhs op rhs     est     se pval            confint    est_sig
#> 1     Means.y.aux1   y ~1   1  153.67   2.88 0.00   [148.02, 159.32]  153.67***
#> 2 Variances.y.aux1   y ~~   y 2496.42 203.70 0.00 [2097.16, 2895.67] 2496.42***
#> 3     Means.y.aux2   y ~1   1  160.66   3.82 0.00   [153.17, 168.15]  160.66***
#> 4 Variances.y.aux2   y ~~   y 3076.16 299.84 0.00 [2488.48, 3663.83] 3076.16***
#>   pval_std  confint_std free        name lboundmet uboundmet std_est std_se col
#> 1     0.00 [2.80, 3.35] TRUE aux1.M[1,1]     FALSE     FALSE    3.08   0.14   y
#> 2     0.00 [1.00, 1.00] TRUE aux1.S[1,1]     FALSE     FALSE    1.00   0.00   y
#> 3     0.00 [2.59, 3.20] TRUE aux2.M[1,1]     FALSE     FALSE    2.90   0.16   y
#> 4     0.00 [1.00, 1.00] TRUE aux2.S[1,1]     FALSE     FALSE    1.00   0.00   y
#>   matrix openmx_label row group ci_type  Category
#> 1      M  aux1.M[1,1]   1  aux1    Wald     Means
#> 2      S  aux1.S[1,1]   y  aux1    Wald Variances
#> 3      M  aux2.M[1,1]   1  aux2    Wald     Means
#> 4      S  aux2.S[1,1]   y  aux2    Wald Variances

The estimates describe class-specific distal means. They do not by themselves test whether the means differ. For an omnibus and pairwise comparison, use lr_test(); compare the means (M) rather than the entire auxiliary model.

lr_test(bch_mean, compare = "M")
#> BCH test for equality across classes
#> 
#> Overall likelihood ratio test:
#>  LL_baseline LL_restricted LL_dif df    p
#>         5491          5494    2.1  1 0.14
#> 
#> Pairwise comparisons using likelihood ratio tests:
#>  Model1 Model2 LL_baseline LL_restricted LL_dif df    p
#>    aux1   aux2        5491          5494    2.1  1 0.14

One crucial limitation of the BCH approach is that its standard errors are not valid, so be careful drawing inferences about parameters in these distal models.

Binary or ordinal distal outcome

For a binary distal outcome, BCH() estimates class-specific thresholds. The function table_prob() represents these in the more interpretable response probability scale:

sex <- ordered(df$sexpatient, levels = c("male", "female"))
bch_sex <- BCH(lpa_model, data = sex)
table_prob(bch_sex)
#>   Variable Category Probability group
#> 1        y        1        0.51  aux1
#> 2        y        2        0.49  aux1
#> 3        y        1        0.46  aux2
#> 4        y        2        0.54  aux2

A class-specific regression model

The model argument accepts lavaan-style syntax. This example investigates whether the classes differ in the effect of distance on frequency of visits. If we request the "matrix" column of the output, you can see that the regression coefficients live in the "A" matrix (asymmetric effects, in other words: regressions). A likelihood ratio test of the "A" matrix thus investigates whether the regression coefficient differs significantly between the two classes:

df_aux <- df[, c("freqvisit", "distance"), drop = FALSE]
df_aux$freqvisit <- as.numeric(df_aux$freqvisit)
bch_reg <- BCH(lpa_model,
               model = "freqvisit ~ distance",
               data = df_aux)
table_results(bch_reg, columns = c("label", "est_sig", "se", "pval", "confint", "group", "matrix"))
lr_test(bch_reg, compare = "A")
#>                                     label       lhs op       rhs     est     se

Two-step maximum likelihood

A different approach to auxiliary analysis is the two_step() procedure. It first estimates the latent class model, then fixes its parameters and adds class-specific auxiliary models (whose parameters are free). This prevents the auxiliary model from influencing the class solution. Unlike BCH, the auxiliary outcomes enter the likelihood directly; posterior class probabilities can therefore change even though measurement parameters stay fixed.

The interface of this function is similar to BCH():

two_mean <- two_step(lpa_model, data = df$distance)
table_results(two_mean, columns = NULL)

Ordinary standard errors for the auxiliary model are also not valid, but tidySEM replaces them with corrected two-step standard errors. These are available in the attribute attr(model, "se_robust"), and table_results() shows them by default.

attr(two_mean, "se_robust")
#>        label  se     type
#> 1 aux1_S_1_1 217 adjusted
#> 2 aux1_M_1_1   3 adjusted
#> 3 aux2_S_1_1 318 adjusted
#> 4 aux2_M_1_1   4 adjusted

For a custom auxiliary RAM model, the syntax can include multiple outcomes and regressions:

two_reg <- two_step(
  lpa_model,
  model = "freqvisit ~ distance",
  data = df_aux
)
table_results(two_reg)

Pseudo-class draws and pooling

The pseudo-class approach accounts for classification uncertainty by repeatedly drawing one class for each observation according to its posterior probabilities. Thus, a person with posterior probabilities (.05,.93,.02)(.05,.93,.02) will be assigned to class 2 in most replications, but occasionally to class 1 or 3. Conversely, a participant with posterior class probabilities (.45,.35,.20)(.45,.35,.20) will be assigned to each of the three classes in many replications.

The auxiliary model is fitted in each completed dataset, and the results are pooled. This propagates classification uncertainty through the draws. Increasing the number of draws reduces Monte Carlo error.

Compare distal means

Here we use lm() with a factor-coded class variable and no intercept, yielding one coefficient per class. The model expression is evaluated in each pseudo-class dataset.

set.seed(2027)
pseudo_mean <- pseudo_class(
  x = lpa_model,
  model = lm(distance ~ I(factor(class)) - 1, data = data),
  data = df[, "distance", drop = FALSE],
  m = 20
)
pseudo_mean
#>                term estimate std.error statistic  df  p.value
#> 1 I(factor(class))1      154       3.2        48 330 5.7e-150
#> 2 I(factor(class))2      160       4.0        40 251 1.7e-111

Use RAM syntax

The pseudo_class() approach also accepts auxiliary models expressed using lavaan syntax. If the model does not explicitly reference class, the function treats class as a grouping variable.

set.seed(2028)
pseudo_ram <- pseudo_class(
  x = lpa_model,
  model = "distance ~ 1",
  data = df[, "distance", drop = FALSE],
  m = 20
)
pseudo_ram
#>                   term estimate    se statistic  df df_complete   pvalue
#> 1     Means.distance.1      154   3.0      51.1 441         509 1.7e-187
#> 2 Variances.distance.1     2560 216.5      11.8 425         509  4.4e-28
#> 3     Means.distance.2      160   3.9      41.1 420         509 3.8e-149
#> 4 Variances.distance.2     2990 303.0       9.9 412         509  9.3e-21

Predicting class membership

So far, we have treated class membership as an explanatory grouping for auxiliary outcomes. Sometimes the research question instead asks which external variables predict class membership. These are not the same estimands: differences in a distal mean do not supply the coefficients of a multinomial regression adjusted for other predictors.

For example, a multinomial model can be fitted across pseudo-class draws using nnet::multinom():

set.seed(2030)
pseudo_pred <- pseudo_class(
  x = lpa_model,
  model = function(data) {
    nnet::multinom(class ~ distance + freqvisit,
                   data = data, trace = FALSE)
  },
  data = df_aux,
  m = 20
)
pseudo_pred
#>            term estimate std.error statistic  df p.value
#> 1 (Intercept).1   -0.480    0.4785     -1.00 274    0.32
#> 2    distance.1    0.002    0.0019      1.04 212    0.30
#> 3   freqvisit.1   -0.050    0.0901     -0.55 389    0.58

The coefficients describe conditional associations with class membership relative to a reference class.

Reporting auxiliary analyses

A report should identify the measurement indicators, selected number of classes, classification quality, auxiliary-variable role, estimation method, and treatment of uncertainty. Report class-specific estimates and their units, as well as uncertainty intervals. Mention what kind of standard errors you used, and whether they are valid. For comparisons across classes via likelihood ratio test, state which parameters were constrained.
